entries.answer: Code is the text a programmer writes, and the word is also a verb meaning to write it, which is a fairly recent extension. It is worth separating from a program, since code is one language and a program is the behaviour, and the same behaviour can be reached by different code. The word also carries a slightly negative connotation about quality, where bad code is what people say when something has been written carelessly.

patterns: is syntax the same as grammar
entries.answer: Syntax is the set of rules governing how a program is written down, and it is deliberately separate from meaning, so a sentence can be grammatically perfect and still say nothing. This is the difference between a syntax error and a runtime fault, and it decides when a mistake is caught: a syntax error is found before anything runs, while a wrong result is found later or never. Every language has its own syntax, and none of them is a superset of another.

entries.answer: A compiler translates a whole program into another program, usually machine code, before any of it runs, and the result is a separate artefact that can be run repeatedly. An interpreter instead executes the source line by line as it reads it, so there is no separate artefact and errors surface at the moment they are reached. Most modern languages use a mixture, compiling to an intermediate form and running a virtual machine over it, which is why the distinction now describes a spectrum.

entries.answer: A library is a set of code someone else wrote that you call rather than rewrite, and the word assumes the pieces are independent enough to be picked individually. A framework is the stronger case, where the structure is decided for you and your code fills in the gaps, and that is why the saying about frameworks differing in size is half true. The practical question is whether you need one particular job done or a whole application built, and the two lead to opposite answers.

patterns: what is a comment in code
entries.answer: A comment is text in a program that is ignored by the language, and it exists for the reader rather than the machine, which is the whole reason the distinction matters. What belongs in one is a genuine judgement, because anything obvious is noise, and the best comments explain why a decision was made rather than restating what the line does. The same word also means a remark, and in a review the verb means to leave those remarks in the code.
